title: Ultrasound‐modified asphaltene from heavy oil: A sustainable adsorbent for dye removal in wastewater
content:
Abstract

Asphaltenes are highly aromatic, polar, and undesirable components present in crude oil, possessing a higher percentage in heavier crude oil. In this work, the influence of ultrasound on asphaltene from heavy oil was investigated, and found that asphaltene size was reduced from 10 to 1 μm at an ultrasound set power of 100%. SEM analysis showed that treated sonicated raw asphaltene (TRasp-100) has more voids and cracks than treated raw asphaltene (TRasp), while BET indicated a higher surface area (40.952 m2/g) for TRasp-100 due to ultrasound, with NMR confirming structural changes, and FTIR showing no significant functional group alterations after sonication. Due to its rich carbon composition, asphaltene was acid-modified and applied as a potent adsorbent for eliminating methyl orange (MO) from wastewater. It was found that ultrasound-treated asphaltene achieved 87% removal of MO at 50 mg/L concentration under pH 4, 313 K, and 90 min contact time, whereas raw asphaltene adsorbed 69% under the same condition. The equilibrium data for ultrasound-influenced asphaltene were evaluated from Freundlich and Langmuir isotherms. To analyze the kinetics, pseudo-first-order, pseudo-second-order, and intraparticle diffusion equations were applied. The thermodynamic parameters ΔH0$$ \varDelta {H}^0 $$, ΔG0$$ \varDelta {G}^0 $$, and Δs0$$ \varDelta {s}^0 $$ were evaluated in this study.
